item.title: How China got access to Nvidia's AI chips despite rules to stop them
item.description: About a year ago, President Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, drawing criticism from experts who said the chips would help jumpstart China's military modernization and erode ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: AI chips are a central battleground in the US-China technology race. To preserve its lead, in recent years Washington has imposed and revised rules to restrict China's access to advanced semiconductors and chipmaking technology, while balancing national security concerns with trade considerations. The drama around Nvidia, the top US exporter of AI chips to China, has thrust those rules into the spotlight. Delving into the resulting regulations is a quagmire. Export control rules are often likened to the US tax code in their complexity and constant revision.Here are some basics for understanding what's legal, and what's not, when it comes to China's access to US AI chips: When did the US start to restrict chips to China?   In October 2022, the US unveiled sweeping restrictions on advanced chips to China, marking the biggest shift in US policy toward exporting technology to China in decades. A year later, it tightened the rules to capture more chips and stop chip designers such as Nvidia from selling products engineered to fall just below the performance thresholds of the earlier restrictions. It also expanded the restrictions to countries in the Middle East and restricted chips to overseas companies headquartered in China. In January 2025, the Biden administration extended the restrictions globally, imposing a worldwide license requirement. But in May, days before it was set to take effect, the Trump administration announced it would not enforce that rule. The Trump administration only formally rescinded and replaced the rule last week, leaving a gap that allowed data center capacity to proliferate in countries such as Singapore, where Chinese companies could rent computing power remotely to train and deploy AI models. Did Megaspeed, the Singapore cloud company whose former executive allegedly had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, operate legally?  For over two years, authorities have been investigating whether Megaspeed diverted chips to China, which would be illegal. But companies in countries including Singapore were allowed to buy advanced AI chips for their data centers license-free until the US issued a new rule last week cutting off that practice. Megaspeed likely won't be getting any more chips. It was added to a US trade blacklist this week, along with its Thai and Malaysian subsidiaries, essentially blocking shipments. Nvidia also said it cut off sales to Megaspeed in June 2025. Are Nvidia's shipments of AI chips to China legal?  About a year ago, President Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, drawing criticism from experts who said the chips would help jumpstart China's military modernization and erode the US lead in AI. The H200 chip is one of Nvidia's more advanced chips, but not top-of-the-line. Nvidia cannot simply ship the chips to Chinese companies that pay for them. Nvidia must apply for licenses from the US Department of Commerce, which has issued them since last spring on a case-by-case basis. Last week, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released licensing data showing the Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026. What does the new Trump administration rule do?  Last week, the Trump administration issued a new regulation, adding license requirements for five countries including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, in an effort to crack down on chips being smuggled into China. Prior to that, the chip-based license requirement generally applied to countries like Russia that raise national security concerns, along with companies headquartered in arms-embargoed countries. Now they also apply to Southeast Asian countries viewed as transshipment points with a high risk for illegal diversion to China. The rule also clamped down on AI chip sales to non-US data centers that supply a high volume of computing power to Chinese-headquartered firms. How big a problem is chip smuggling?  For years, Nvidia's Huang has said there is no evidence of chip smuggling to China. But that assertion, which experts already viewed skeptically, was further questioned in March when US prosecutors charged three people associated with California-based AI server maker Super Micro Computer, including its co-founder, in a scheme to divert about $2.5 billion of US technology into China, including AI servers packed with Nvidia AI chips. Critics say Nvidia has tried to minimize a well-known risk. Huang once said Nvidia's sophisticated Grace Blackwell AI chip platform weighed nearly two tons (1.8 metric tons) and could not fit into a pocket or backpack. But servers are not smuggled in backpacks. They are routed through third countries and intermediary companies. Supporters say Nvidia may not have had verified evidence of diversion and that the company cannot keep tabs on all its products after they're sold. Can Nvidia track its chips to see where they end up?  Nvidia has built location verification technology that could indicate which country its chips are operating in, the company confirmed in December 2025. It has offered the feature as a software option for customers. But the company has opposed proposed legislation that would require location verification and diversion reporting for advanced AI processors. A measure known as the Chip Security Act is among several export control bills that gained new momentum in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, and may be included in the National Defense Authorization Act that Congress is expected to pass next month.

item.title: Uber appoints former Zomato CEO Rakesh Ranjan as India, South Asia head
item.description: The appointment comes months after the position became vacant when Prabhjeet Singh left in June 2026 to head OpenAI's India operations as managing director ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Uber said on Thursday it had appointed Rakesh Ranjan as its president for India and South Asia, effective January 4, 2027.The appointment comes months after the position became vacant when Prabhjeet Singh left in June 2026 to head OpenAI's India operations as managing director.Ranjan is currently the chief executive officer of Allen Online, the digital arm of coaching institute Allen Career Institute.He previously spent eight years at Eternal, then known as Zomato, joining in 2017 and going on to become CEO of its food ordering and delivery business.According to Uber, India is its third-largest market by trips, behind the US and Brazil, and its second-largest by number of earners globally.

item.title: Farmers sell paddy stubble to biomass firms, cut farm fires in Punjab
item.description: The shift offers a potential solution to stubble burning, which has persisted despite years of government efforts to stamp it out ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / Agriculture / Farmers sell paddy stubble to biomass firms, cut farm fires in Punjab

Farmers sell paddy stubble to biomass firms, cut farm fires in Punjab The shift offers a potential solution to stubble burning, which has persisted despite years of government efforts to stamp it out

More Punjab farmers are finding that straw once treated as waste can generate income, reducing the incentive to burn it (Photo: Sarthak Choudhury)

Reuters SEDHA SINGH WALA 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 26 2026 | 8:12 AM IST

Listen to This Article

For years, 60-year-old farmer Rajinder Singh burned his paddy stubble after the harvest, one of thousands of fires across India's Punjab state each autumn. Now, his crop waste is trucked to a biomass plant, generating power and village incomes instead of smoke. The shift offers a potential solution to stubble burning, which has persisted despite years of government efforts to stamp it out. Such fires have contributed to the toxic smog that blankets the capital Delhi and much of northern India each winter, making it one of the most polluted areas in the world. "Our earnings have improved considerably through this work," Singh said, speaking in his Sedha Singh Wala village in Punjab. "Earlier we used to burn the stubble. Now many families are getting employment from it."   More Punjab farmers are finding that straw once treated as waste can generate income, reducing the incentive to burn it. Punjab recorded 5,114 farm fires during the 2025 paddy-harvesting season, down 53% from 2024 and 86% from 2023, according to government estimates. Also Read

Shiromani Akali Dal back in NDA fold, to fight Punjab polls with BJP

Stubble burning numbers fall sharply, but satellite blind spots cloud data premium

States' combined fiscal deficit seen narrowing to 2.9% of GDP in FY27

Datanomics: Delhi's AQI improves after hitting 5-year high on Diwali premium

Centre allows transfer of prisoners between Chandigarh, other states

But the dramatic fall has yet to translate into noticeably cleaner air in Delhi. The capital's air quality again reached hazardous levels in mid-November this year, underscoring both the multiple sources of its pollution and the limited scale of the biomass industry. "Biomass-based projects are financially sound and genuinely effective," said Pratima Singh, a director at policy and research firm iFOREST. "But right now they're operating at a fraction of the scale needed, so their impact isn't yet visible in Delhi's air." MORE INCOMES, JOBS In Punjab's Faridkot district, a network of farmers, machinery operators and biomass power producers have emerged to collect paddy straw and turn it into fuel for electricity generation. Farmers and analysts say the business is also creating jobs, and boosting incomes, but government incentives are needed to expand it enough to make a meaningful dent. Amandeep Singh Gill, who processes paddy straw into feedstock for power plants, provides work for tractor operators, drivers and labourers, providing livelihoods for as many as 70 families. The business requires substantial investment. Gill said his operation cost about 45 million rupees ($484,340) to set up and can generate annual turnover of 70 million to 80 million rupees. The collected straw eventually reaches an 18-megawatt biomass power plant operated by SAEL Industries Ltd, where agricultural waste is used to generate electricity. SAEL, the country's largest procurer of agricultural residue, is buying 2 million tonnes this year, a fraction of the roughly 750 million tonnes of agricultural waste generated in India each year. A minimum support price for paddy straw and standardised procurement contracts could help expand the industry and meet the government's target of utilising 10 million tonnes of straw per year, iFOREST's Singh said. That, she said, could further reduce farm fires, although a much larger expansion would be needed before the impact becomes visible in Delhi's air.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: Ajay Devgn moves court against FDA notice over Vimal cardamom ads
item.description: India restricts advertising for liquor and tobacco but officials have for years also frowned upon the use of indirect means, called surrogate advertising ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / Ajay Devgn moves court against FDA notice over Vimal cardamom ads

Ajay Devgn moves court against FDA notice over Vimal cardamom ads India restricts advertising for liquor and tobacco but officials have for years also frowned upon the use of indirect means, called surrogate advertising

Devgn in his filing argues cardamom has not been prohibited in the state and "there is no bar in endorsing a product which is not prohibited"

Reuters NEW DELHI 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 26 2026 | 8:04 AM IST

Listen to This Article

An advertisement for cardamom is at the centre of a legal spat between a Bollywood actor and India's most prominent food commissioner, with a court ruling set to shape how far companies can go in indirectly advertising brands whose promotion is restricted. India restricts advertising for liquor and tobacco but officials have for years also frowned upon the use of indirect means, called surrogate advertising, by companies in such sectors promoting their brands in the guise of sodas, water or glassware. While companies say these are genuine businesses in their own right whose advertising cannot be curbed, health officials say the advertisements are aimed at generating recall of the parent brand whose publicity is restricted. Since 2024, India has been trying to finalise stringent guidelines to prohibit such advertisements outright.   In the case involving Bollywood stars, actor Ajay Devgn has sued the food authority of Maharashtra state, arguing he has been wrongly told to stop appearing in advertisements for Vimal cardamom packs, according to a non-public court filing dated October 15 reviewed by Reuters. The state, whose food safety commissioner Tukaram Mundhe has become a national sensation for his aggressive stance on public health, asked Bollywood stars Devgn, Shah Rukh Khan and Tiger Shroff in August to stop appearing in advertisements promoting Vimal cardamom, arguing the brand is mostly known for its betel nut mix, or pan masala, which is banned in the state. Also Read

Maharashtra FDA warns gyms against unauthorised sale of health supplements

FDA suspends NSCI food licence; Mumbai University canteen fined ₹1 lakh

Maha FDA suspends Amazon, BigBasket Pune dark stores over safety violations

Maharashtra FDA seizes food stock worth ₹63.45 crore ahead of Diwali

Japan protests as Putin orders takeover of Japan Tobacco's Russia unit

The spat in the High Court in Mumbai could set a precedent, New Delhi-based lawyer Anuj Tiwari said. "The case will test both the fairness of the department's process before it imposes restrictions ... and the parameters for deciding what counts as indirect advertising," he said. COURT SPAT ON CARDAMOM AD In the advertisement available on Vimal Cardamom's YouTube page and posted two years ago, the Bollywood stars are seen celebrating, throwing saffron at each other after Devgn consumes the product. The Hindi-language advertisement has 107 million views, while clips dubbed in other Indian languages have garnered millions more. "Ajay, Shahrukh, and Tiger played saffron Holi like crazy and drenched the entire community in saffron!" says the advertisement's description, referring to the Hindu festival of colour. Devgn in his filing argues cardamom has not been prohibited in the state and "there is no bar in endorsing a product which is not prohibited". Devgn did not respond to Reuters queries. Mundhe told Reuters the state believes the advertisements are against public health interests, and the state is separately reviewing responses submitted by Khan and Shroff, although Reuters could not ascertain details of their submissions. Dushyant Mahant, a lawyer for PB Agro, which holds the licence to make Vimal cardamom and pan masala, told Reuters the allegations were futile as the company does not promote Vimal in Maharashtra and only advertises the product via nationally televised broadcasts that cannot be restricted geographically. Industry estimates show India's pan masala market was worth around $5 billion last year. Health experts say the product is a leading cause of oral fibrosis that often progresses to oral cancer. While Maharashtra bans it, Vimal's tobacco-free pan masala sachets in other states cost around ₹5 (5.4 US cents). But they are often consumed with chewing tobacco, sold at kiosks as "twin packs" - a pan masala sachet alongside a tiny pouch of unbranded tobacco. An adverse ruling in Devgn's case could affect Bollywood stars as endorsements can amount to up to 30% of an actor's earnings, and promoting tobacco-linked products is more lucrative than other advertisements, said Suresh Mathew, a Mumbai-based screenwriter. "Most actors know if a product is a surrogate for another product," he added. "There are cases where certain actors have refused to lend their name to a product that they feel is harmful."
